title: Vanka
text:
Vanka Zhukov, a boy of nine, had been sent three months earlier to Moscow as an apprentice to the shoemaker Alyakhin. On Christmas Eve, while his master and the workmen were at church, he took out a crumpled sheet of paper and a rusty pen and began a letter to his grandfather, Konstantin Makaritch, a night watchman on a country estate.

He wrote that he had no father and no mother, that his grandfather was all he had. His master had pulled him by the hair into the yard and thrashed him for falling asleep while rocking the baby. The mistress had poked him in the face with a herring. There was nothing to eat but bread in the morning and porridge at night. "Dear grandfather, for God's sake take me away from here, home to the village."

Between lines he remembered his grandfather: his laughter, the frosty nights, the dogs, going with him to cut a Christmas tree, the young lady at the big house who had taught him to read.

He folded the letter and addressed the envelope: "To grandfather in the village." Then, after a moment's thought, he added the name: "Konstantin Makaritch." He ran out and dropped it in the post box, and that night he fell asleep happy, dreaming of his grandfather reading his letter to the cook by the stove.
lesson: A child sent away to work or to cope alone still needs home more than anything. Make sure the children in your life know where to reach you.
people: Vanka Zhukov, his grandfather Konstantin Makaritch
